opus-5.5.text:
I think the ratio between full attention and sliding-window attention isn't a fixed number. It's something you have to keep revisiting as the model scales, and as your target workloads change.

The basic intuition is simple. Sliding-window layers are cheap. Their KV cache is bounded, their compute is local, and they handle most of the "short-range" work in language well: syntax, local coherence, nearby references. Full-attention layers are expensive, especially at long context, but they're the only place where the model can do genuine global retrieval, like pulling a fact from 100K tokens back or tying together information across a long document or a long agent trajectory.

So the question becomes: how many global layers do you actually need to preserve long-range capability, and where do you put them?

As models get larger, my sense is that you can often afford a *more aggressive* hybrid ratio, meaning a smaller fraction of full-attention layers. A bigger model has more capacity per layer, and the local layers get better at compressing and passing information upward, so a few well-placed global layers can do a lot of the retrieval work. But there's a catch. If you push the ratio too far, the model can look fine on standard benchmarks and short-context evals, and then quietly degrade on things like multi-hop retrieval in long context or long-horizon reasoning, where errors compound. So you can't judge the ratio by perplexity alone. You need evals that specifically stress long-range dependency.

A few practical things matter a lot in my experience:

First, **placement**. Interleaving global layers periodically tends to work better than clustering them, because each segment of local layers gets a chance to "refresh" global information.

Second, **window size interacts with the ratio**. A larger sliding window lets you get away with fewer global layers, but then you lose some of the efficiency you were trying to gain. It's a joint design choice, not two independent knobs.

Third, **the details around attention stability**, things like attention sinks or how you handle positional encoding in the local versus global layers, can make a surprisingly big difference. Sometimes a hybrid config that seems to fail is actually failing because of one of these small details, not because the ratio itself is wrong.

And finally, I think the deciding factor increasingly is **inference economics**, especially for agentic use cases. When models run long multi-turn tasks with huge contexts, KV cache memory and decoding speed become the real bottleneck. So the balance is really a three-way trade-off between capability, training cost, and serving cost. The "right" answer depends on what you want the model to be good at. For an agent model that lives in long contexts, I'd be quite careful not to cut global attention too much. For a model mostly serving short interactions, you can be much more aggressive.

r001.rationale: It discusses using a smaller fraction of full-attention layers as models grow, but does not propose increasing depth by adding sliding-window layers while keeping the full-attention count fixed.

r002.rationale: It frames the choice around the ratio and workload trade-offs, without suggesting that the absolute number of full-attention layers matters more than their proportion.

r003.rationale: It says bigger models may need a smaller fraction of full-attention layers, but does not connect that possibility to both larger parameter counts and more attention heads.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it less as a fixed ratio and more as a question of what each type of layer is actually for.

Full attention is where the model does the hard, global work — pulling in information from anywhere in the context, resolving long-range dependencies, doing the kind of retrieval that a sliding window simply cannot do. Sliding-window layers are much cheaper, both in compute and especially in KV cache, and they're very good at the local, syntactic, "what came just before this" kind of modeling that makes up most of language. So the natural design is to interleave them: let a minority of global layers handle the long-range mixing and let the cheap local layers do the bulk of the work in between.

What changes as models scale is the pressure from the KV cache. When you get to very long contexts, the cache for full-attention layers dominates memory and inference cost almost regardless of how big the MLPs are. That's what pushes the ratio toward fewer global layers — maybe one in four, one in six, or even sparser. Our experience is that you can push this quite far before quality degrades, as long as the global layers are positioned well. Too few, or placed only at the very top, and the model loses the ability to actually route information to where the local layers can use it. You want them spread through the depth so there are repeated opportunities for global information to enter and then be refined locally.

The other thing I'd say is that the right balance depends heavily on the training data and what you're optimizing for. If you care about long-context reasoning and retrieval — agents, code, long documents — you need more global capacity, or you need to compensate with things like larger windows in the local layers or some form of compressed global memory. If most of your workload is short-context chat, you can be very aggressive. So I don't think there's one answer. The honest answer is that it's an empirical tradeoff, and we try to make the decision based on measured long-context performance at a fixed inference budget rather than on any theoretical argument.

r001.rationale: The response recommends interleaving mostly local layers with fewer global layers, but does not propose increasing depth by adding sliding-window layers while keeping the full-attention count fixed.

r002.rationale: It discusses a lower proportion of global layers and their placement, but does not say their absolute number matters more than their proportion.

r003.rationale: It links fewer global layers to long-context KV-cache pressure, but does not connect a lower full-attention proportion to larger parameter counts and more attention heads.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance depends on what you want the model to retain over long distances. Sliding-window attention handles local interactions at a lower cost, while full attention lets information move directly across the entire context. The question is how often you need that global communication.

As models get larger and deeper, it’s reasonable to explore using more sliding-window layers, with full-attention layers at selected depths. But I wouldn’t assume that increasing model size automatically means you can reduce the proportion of full attention. More capacity doesn’t necessarily compensate for limited access to information.

I’d treat the ratio and placement as empirical design choices. You need to measure both efficiency and whether the model can connect information that is far apart, especially when a task requires several such connections. The useful balance is the one that preserves those capabilities at the context lengths you actually care about.

r001.rationale: It proposes exploring more sliding-window layers with full-attention layers at selected depths, but does not say to hold the number of full-attention layers fixed.

r002.rationale: It discusses the proportion of full-attention layers but does not suggest their absolute number matters more than that proportion.

r003.rationale: It says larger models do not necessarily justify reducing the full-attention proportion; it does not suggest that more parameters and attention heads support a lower proportion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a balance between local processing and global communication. Sliding-window attention lets you do a lot of the local work efficiently, while full attention gives information a path across the entire context.

As models get larger, you may have more room to use sliding-window layers, because you have more layers in which to mix information. But I wouldn’t assume there’s a fixed ratio that should change monotonically with model size. The right balance also depends on context length and what the model needs to do. A model can look very good on average and still struggle when it has to connect two pieces of information that are far apart.

So I would tune both the number and the placement of full-attention layers, then test whether the model actually uses distant context. The goal is to keep enough global communication to preserve capability while making the rest of the computation more efficient.

r001.rationale: It says larger models may have more room for sliding-window layers, but does not propose adding them while holding the number of full-attention layers fixed.

r002.rationale: It recommends tuning the number and placement of full-attention layers, but does not say their absolute number matters more than their proportion.

r003.rationale: It does not connect parameter count or attention-head count to using a lower proportion of full-attention layers.
